prompt: After `ALTER KEYSPACE shop` raises the replication factor from 1 to 3, Cassandra warns that a full repair is needed. Why?

choices.text: The keyspace is locked until a repair confirms the new setting
choices.why: Nothing is locked; the stock table was created and written straight after.

choices.text: Existing rows are not copied to the new replicas by the ALTER
choices.why: Right. Two of the three nodes now responsible for each old partition have never seen it.

choices.text: New writes go to one replica until the repair finishes
choices.why: New writes go to all three at once; it is the old rows that are missing.

choices.text: Repair rebuilds the ring with more tokens per node
choices.why: Tokens are unchanged; repair compares and copies data.

prompt: Where is the replication factor set?

choices.text: On the keyspace
choices.why: Right: WITH replication = {...} on CREATE or ALTER KEYSPACE.

choices.text: On each query, with CONSISTENCY
choices.why: CONSISTENCY sets how many copies must answer, not how many exist.

choices.text: On each table, beside the primary key
choices.why: Tables inherit it from their keyspace.

choices.text: In each node's cassandra.yaml
choices.why: It is a schema setting shared by the cluster, not a node file.

prompt: What does `cqlsh` answer to `CONSISTENCY` with no argument in a new session?

choices.text: Current consistency level is QUORUM.
choices.why: QUORUM is a common choice in applications, but cqlsh does not start there.

choices.text: Current consistency level is ALL.
choices.why: ALL would make every query fail with one node down.

choices.text: Current consistency level is LOCAL_QUORUM.
choices.why: Some drivers default to LOCAL_ONE or LOCAL_QUORUM; cqlsh said ONE.

choices.text: Current consistency level is ONE.
choices.why: Right, as the lab showed: one replica's answer is enough unless you say otherwise.

prompt: A team keeps one data centre today and plans a second next year. Which keyspace replication fits, and why?

choices.text: SimpleStrategy, because one data centre is all it has to describe
choices.why: It works today, and moving off it later is an ALTER plus a repair.

choices.text: Either one, since replication can be switched off while the second centre is added
choices.why: Replication is never switched off; the strategy decides where the copies go.

choices.text: NetworkTopologyStrategy with dc1 named, so the second centre is a new entry
choices.why: Right. Copies are counted per data centre by name, and LOCAL_QUORUM depends on it.

choices.text: A replication factor of 6 today, so the second centre's copies already exist
choices.why: Three nodes cannot hold six copies of a partition.

prompt: A keyspace has a replication factor of 5. How many replicas must answer a read at QUORUM?
With `c3` stopped, a read at `ALL` answered `Cannot achieve consistency level ALL` at once. What did the coordinator do?

choices.text: Knew from gossip that only 2 replicas were alive, and refused without sending
choices.why: Right: Unavailable, with required_replicas 3 and alive_replicas 2.

choices.text: Sent the read to all three and waited for c3 until the timeout
choices.why: That would be a timeout error after seconds; this came at once.

choices.text: Read from two replicas and reported their answers disagreed
choices.why: Disagreement is repaired, not reported as unavailable.

choices.text: Returned the row from c1 and logged a warning
choices.why: ALL never answers with fewer than all replicas.

prompt: With `c3` down, an `UPDATE` at `QUORUM` succeeds. To which replicas was the write sent?

choices.text: To any two chosen at random, possibly including c3
choices.why: The coordinator knows c3 is down and sends to the live ones.

choices.text: To c1 alone, the coordinator
choices.why: That would be one acknowledgement, not a quorum.

choices.text: To all three, including c3, which stores it on disk while stopped
choices.why: A stopped node receives nothing; lesson 19 shows what keeps its missed writes.

choices.text: To the two that are up, c1 and c2
choices.why: Right. A write goes to every live replica; QUORUM waited for two acknowledgements and had them.

prompt: With a replication factor of 3, match each level to the most nodes that can be down while it still answers.
With two nodes down, `ONE` read `0` from `c1`, the value written at `QUORUM`. Why can't you rely on `ONE` returning the latest value in general?

choices.text: Because ONE reads from a cache that is refreshed every few seconds
choices.why: There is no such cache in the read path here; it reads a replica.

choices.text: Because it trusts one replica, and nothing says that one has the last write
choices.why: Right. c1 happened to be one of the two that took the write.

choices.text: Because ONE ignores timestamps and returns the first value found
choices.why: With one answer there is nothing to compare; the problem is which replica answered.

choices.text: Because a read at ONE is refused while any node is down
choices.why: It answered with two nodes down.

prompt: In `nodetool status`, what does `DN` mean for `c3`?

choices.text: Down and normal: still in the ring, not answering
choices.why: Right. It keeps its tokens; the others know it is not answering.

choices.text: Decommissioned: removed from the ring and its data handed over
choices.why: A decommissioned node disappears from the list.

choices.text: Data node, as opposed to a seed
choices.why: The two letters are status and state.

choices.text: Draining: finishing its writes before stopping
choices.why: D is Down; draining is not one of the states shown.

prompt: RF is 3. A team writes at `ONE` and reads at `QUORUM`. Does a read always see the last acknowledged write?

choices.text: Yes, because QUORUM reads a majority
choices.why: A majority of reads can still miss the single replica that has the write.

choices.text: No, because QUORUM reads skip the coordinator's own copy
choices.why: The coordinator's copy can be one of those read; the arithmetic is the reason.

choices.text: Yes, as long as no node is down
choices.why: Even with all up, the write may not have reached the other two yet.

choices.text: No: 1 + 2 is not greater than 3
choices.why: Right. The two replicas read can both be ones the write has not reached.

prompt: Which pair of levels, with RF 3, both sees the last write and keeps working with one node down?

choices.text: ONE writes, ALL reads
choices.why: It sees the last write, and any node down stops every read.

choices.text: ONE writes, ONE reads
choices.why: It survives two nodes down, and 1 + 1 does not exceed 3.

choices.text: QUORUM writes, QUORUM reads
choices.why: Right: 2 + 2 > 3, and each needs only two of three.

choices.text: ALL writes, ONE reads
choices.why: It sees the last write, and any node down stops every write.

prompt: A cluster has three replicas in São Paulo and three in Lisbon. The application in São Paulo uses `QUORUM`. What does every request pay?
hint: How many replicas is a quorum of six?

choices.text: Nothing extra, because the coordinator answers from its own region first
choices.why: A quorum of 6 is 4, and São Paulo has only 3.

choices.text: A wait for at least one answer from Lisbon, the cross-ocean round trip
choices.why: Right. LOCAL_QUORUM would need 2 of the 3 local replicas instead.

choices.text: A refusal, since QUORUM is not allowed with two data centres
choices.why: It is allowed; it is slow.

choices.text: Six acknowledgements on every write
choices.why: That would be ALL.

prompt: In a cluster with one data centre per region, the everyday level that keeps reads and writes inside the client's own region is ___.
A `QUORUM` write times out after one replica acknowledged it. What is true afterwards?

choices.text: The write is rolled back on that replica automatically
choices.why: Cassandra has no rollback for a single write.

choices.text: The coordinator retries until it succeeds
choices.why: The client receives the timeout; retrying is the application's decision.

choices.text: No replica has it, since the level was not reached
choices.why: The level decides the answer to the client, not what the replicas stored.

choices.text: The value stays on that replica, and a later read that asks it will find it
choices.why: Right. A failed write is not an undone write.

prompt: Put the four rounds of a lightweight transaction in order, as the trace showed them.
items: PREPARE: claim the right to propose
READ: fetch the current value and check the condition
PROPOSE: agree on the new value
trap: The condition can only be checked once the right to propose is held.

prompt: The second `UPDATE ... IF units = 1` returned `[applied] False` and `units 0`. What should the application do with that?

choices.text: Retry the same statement until it applies
choices.why: It will never apply while units is 0; the condition is the point.

choices.text: Tell the customer the monitor is sold out
choices.why: Right. It lost the race, and the reply says what it lost to.

choices.text: Write units = 0 without the IF, to be sure
choices.why: A plain write bypasses Paxos and can overwrite an agreed value.

choices.text: Read again at ALL to find out who is right
choices.why: The reply already carries the current value.

prompt: A session is at `CONSISTENCY ONE` and two of three nodes are down. A conditional `UPDATE` is refused. Why?

choices.text: Its Paxos rounds use the serial level, which needs a majority
choices.why: Right: Cannot achieve consistency level SERIAL, required 2, alive 1.

choices.text: Conditional writes are only allowed when the session is at QUORUM or above
choices.why: The ordinary level can be ONE; it governs the commit, not the decision.

choices.text: The row was still locked by the earlier plain UPDATE on the same partition
choices.why: Plain writes take no locks.

choices.text: A session at ONE refuses every write while any node of the cluster is down
choices.why: A plain read at ONE answered in the same session.

prompt: Why does the lesson say to keep every write to an LWT-guarded column conditional?

choices.text: Because plain writes to that table are refused
choices.why: They are accepted, which is the danger.

choices.text: Because Cassandra needs a write history to run Paxos
choices.why: Paxos needs a majority, not a history of conditional writes.

choices.text: Because conditional writes are cheaper once the first one has run
choices.why: Each costs four rounds; there is no warm-up.

choices.text: A plain write skips Paxos, so it overwrites what an LWT agreed
choices.why: Right. Only writes that take part in the agreement are ordered by it.

prompt: In the trace, a plain `UPDATE` sent one message to each of the two other replicas. How many messages did the conditional `UPDATE` send to them in total?
RF is 3 and one node is down. Which statements succeed? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A read at QUORUM
choices.why: Right: it needs 2 and has 2.

choices.text: A write at ALL
choices.why: It needs 3 and has 2.

choices.text: A conditional UPDATE
choices.why: Right: SERIAL needs a majority, and 2 of 3 is one.

choices.text: A read at ONE
choices.why: Right: one replica is enough.

choices.text: A read at ALL
choices.why: Unavailable, as the lab showed.

prompt: Two customers buy the last monitor at the same moment, and the shop writes `units = 0` at `QUORUM` for each. What happens?

choices.text: Both succeed, both are told yes, and one monitor is sold twice
choices.why: Right. That is the race only a conditional write closes.

choices.text: The second write fails, because QUORUM detects that the two writes conflict
choices.why: QUORUM counts acknowledgements; it checks no condition.

choices.text: Cassandra merges them into units = -1
choices.why: Each write sets a value; the later timestamp wins.

choices.text: One waits for the other, as in a relational transaction
choices.why: Plain writes take no locks.
